conversation.content: Let's design a web search engine — users type queries, we return relevant web pages. Before we start, what would you want to clarify?
I guess... how many pages are we indexing? And do we need to handle images and videos or just text?
10 billion web pages, text only for now. Results must return in under 200ms. What about query volume?
Oh right, how many searches per second? That would affect the architecture a lot.
100,000 queries per second. Let's start with the high-level components. What are the major pieces of a search engine?
So we need to crawl the web to get the pages. Then index them somehow. And then serve search queries. Three main parts — a crawler, an indexer, and a query service.
Good. Let's start with the indexer — once we have a web page, how do we make it searchable? What data structure enables fast text search?
We could put it in a database and use LIKE queries? Or... I've heard of Elasticsearch. We could use Elasticsearch to index the pages and it handles the search for us.
Elasticsearch is built on a fundamental data structure called an inverted index. Can you describe what that is, even conceptually?

An inverted index... it's like the index in the back of a textbook? Where you look up a word and it tells you which pages it's on. So for each word, we store a list of documents that contain it. When someone searches for 'distributed systems,' we look up 'distributed' and 'systems,' get both lists, and find the documents that appear in both.
Good analogy. Now that intersection might return millions of pages. How do you decide which ones to show first? Why is result #1 better than result #1000?
PageRank? Google uses PageRank. It's based on links — the more links a page has pointing to it, the more important it is. Like if a lot of other websites link to Wikipedia, Wikipedia ranks high.

PageRank is one signal, but it only measures page importance — not relevance to the query. A page could be very important (like Wikipedia's main page) but irrelevant to 'distributed systems.' What measures how relevant a specific page is to a specific query?

Oh, I see. So we need both importance and relevance. For relevance... I guess count how many times the search terms appear on the page? If 'distributed systems' appears 10 times on page A and twice on page B, page A is probably more relevant.

That's term frequency — you're on the right track. But raw term frequency has a flaw. The word 'the' appears 500 times on every page. Does that make every page highly relevant to the query 'the'? There's a concept that adjusts for common words.

Right, common words shouldn't count as much. So we'd weigh rare words higher. If 'distributed' only appears on 0.1% of pages but 'the' appears on 99%, then matching 'distributed' should boost the score way more. Is that IDF — inverse document frequency?
Exactly — TF-IDF combines term frequency with inverse document frequency. Good. Now, 10 billion pages in one inverted index won't fit on a single machine. How do you distribute it?

We'd need to split it across multiple machines. Sharding. Maybe... split the documents? Like documents 1 through 1 billion on shard 1, the next billion on shard 2, and so on. Ten shards for 10 billion documents.
Document-based sharding works. But when a query comes in, what happens? If each shard has a piece of the index, how do you get a complete result?

Oh... we'd have to send the query to all 10 shards, each shard returns its top results, and then we merge them. That's 10 parallel lookups per query. At 100K queries per second, that's a million lookups per second across the shards. Is that too much?

A million lookups per second across 10 shards is 100K per shard — manageable. But each shard needs replicas for availability and load balancing. If each shard has 3 replicas, you have 30 index servers. Now, let's talk about the crawler. How do you crawl 10 billion pages?

A lot of machines crawling in parallel. Start with seed URLs, fetch pages, extract links, add them to a queue, keep going. We'd need to be careful not to overwhelm any single website. And detect duplicates so we don't crawl the same page twice.
How do you detect duplicates efficiently with 10 billion URLs to track?

A hash set? But 10 billion URLs in a hash set would take a huge amount of memory... maybe use a Bloom filter? It's a probabilistic data structure that can tell you 'definitely not seen' or 'probably seen.' It uses way less memory than a full set. Small chance of false positives — we might skip a URL we haven't actually crawled — but that's acceptable.
Good choice with the Bloom filter. What about freshness? How do you know when to re-crawl a page that's changed?

We could check the page periodically. News sites change every few minutes so we'd crawl them often. A personal blog might not change for months. Maybe use the Last-Modified header or... actually I'm not sure how to determine the right re-crawl frequency for each page without wasting resources.

One approach: track how often each page actually changed on past crawls and use that to predict the next update. Pages that change daily get crawled daily; pages that haven't changed in 6 months get crawled monthly. We're out of time — any final thoughts?

I'd add caching for popular queries — 'weather' gets searched millions of times, we shouldn't recompute it every time. And spell correction for typos. I know I struggled with some of the ranking depth — TF-IDF and PageRank are things I should study more deeply.
Appreciate the self-awareness. You showed decent intuition on the building blocks — keep going deeper on the ranking and scaling aspects. Thanks.

strengths: Good textbook analogy for inverted index — showed conceptual understanding
Bloom filter for URL deduplication was a strong practical answer
Self-aware about gaps — not defensive or bluffing
weaknesses: First instinct was 'use Elasticsearch' rather than reasoning from first principles — a senior should go deeper
No capacity estimation at all — didn't calculate index size, memory, or query throughput
Ranking understanding was shallow — needed multiple hints to arrive at TF-IDF
No failure handling discussed — what happens if a shard is down, if the crawler is blocked, if the index is corrupted
No discussion of modern ranking (ML models, BERT, learning-to-rank) expected at senior level
